prompt.context: Your grandfather has just died and left you an oil tanker. You need a valuation for tax purposes and have hired a consultant to tell you what it is worth. There are 3 types of tankers in the world: small, medium, and large. Within each class, every tanker is identical. You have just inherited a medium tanker.
prompt.question: What is the value of the inherited medium oil tanker?

clarifying_info.q: How many tankers of each type exist?
What is the capacity of each tanker type?
clarifying_info.a: Small: 1 unit, Medium: 2 units, Large: 4 units of oil transportation capacity.

clarifying_info.q: How many trips does each tanker make per year?
clarifying_info.a: Each tanker makes 1 trip per year, regardless of size.

clarifying_info.q: What are the operating costs per trip?
What is the demand for oil transportation?
clarifying_info.a: Fixed demand for 500 units of capacity per year. Transport costs are a negligible part of total oil cost structure and demand is completely inelastic.
The market is highly fragmented and therefore competitive.

framework: Determine total supply capacity by tanker type (small, medium, large)
Identify the marginal supplier — the most expensive tanker type needed to meet demand
In a competitive market, price equals the marginal supplier's cost per unit
Calculate revenue for each tanker type at the market-clearing price
Calculate annual profit = revenue minus operating cost for the medium tanker
Value = annual profit divided by discount rate (perpetuity formula)

questions.prompt: What is the total capacity supplied by each tanker type, and which type is the marginal supplier under Scenario I (demand = 500 units)?
questions.guidance: Large tankers supply 100 x 4 = 400 units; medium tankers supply 100 x 2 = 200 units; small tankers supply 100 x 1 = 100 units. With 400 units from large tankers, only 100 more units are needed to reach 500. Medium tankers can supply 200 units but only 100 are needed — so medium tankers are the marginal (price-setting) supplier. Half of medium tankers will be employed at cost-covering rates; the other half sit idle.

math.setup: Total capacity: Large = 100 x 4 = 400 units; Medium = 100 x 2 = 200 units; Small = 100 x 1 = 100 units. Demand = 500 units. 400 (large) + some medium = 500, so 100 units from medium are needed.
steps: Large capacity: 100 tankers x 4 units = 400 units
Remaining demand: 500 - 400 = 100 units, satisfied by medium tankers
Medium tankers are the marginal supplier
math.answer: Medium tankers are the marginal capacity. 50 of the 100 medium tankers will be employed; 50 will sit idle.

questions.prompt: What is the market-clearing price per unit under Scenario I?
questions.guidance: In a competitive market, price equals the marginal cost per unit. The medium tanker costs $75,000 per trip and carries 2 units, so cost per unit = $75,000 / 2 = $37,500.

math.setup: Market-clearing price = marginal cost per unit = operating cost of medium tanker / capacity of medium tanker

questions.prompt: What is the value of the inherited medium tanker under Scenario I (demand = 500 units)?
questions.guidance: Since the medium tanker is the marginal supplier, market price just covers its costs. Annual profit = 0. Value = 0 (or scrap value only). The medium tanker earns revenue of $37,500 x 2 = $75,000 per trip which exactly equals its operating cost of $75,000.

math.setup: Annual profit = Revenue - Operating cost. Revenue = price per unit x capacity. Value = annual profit / discount rate.
math.answer: The medium tanker has zero value (or scrap value only) under Scenario I.

questions.prompt: For completeness: what is the value of a large tanker under Scenario I?
questions.guidance: Large tankers are inframarginal — they earn above-cost returns. Revenue = $37,500 x 4 = $150,000. Profit = $150,000 - $100,000 = $50,000 per year. Value = $50,000 / 0.10 = $500,000.

math.setup: Large tanker: revenue = price x capacity; profit = revenue - cost; value = profit / discount rate
math.answer: Large tanker value = $500,000 under Scenario I.

questions.prompt: (Extension) What is the value of the medium tanker under Scenario II (demand = 650 units)?
questions.guidance: With demand at 650 units: large supplies 400, medium supplies 200, remaining 50 units must come from small tankers. Small tankers are now marginal. Price = small tanker cost per unit = $50,000 / 1 = $50,000 per unit. Medium tanker revenue = $50,000 x 2 = $100,000; profit = $100,000 - $75,000 = $25,000 per year; value = $25,000 / 0.10 = $250,000. Large tanker: revenue = $50,000 x 4 = $200,000; profit = $200,000 - $100,000 = $100,000; value = $100,000 / 0.10 = $1,000,000.

math.setup: Demand = 650 units. Large (400) + Medium (200) = 600, so small tankers supply the remaining 50 units and are marginal.
steps: Marginal supplier: small tanker, cost = $50,000, capacity = 1 unit
math.answer: Medium tanker value = $250,000; Large tanker value = $1,000,000 under Scenario II.

brainstorming.prompt: What factors or additional data would you want to explore to refine the valuation?

categories.name: Revenue/Demand
ideas: Future demand trajectory for oil transportation
Whether demand is truly fixed or responsive to price changes
Geopolitical factors affecting oil trade routes

categories.name: Cost Structure
ideas: Fuel efficiency differences across tanker sizes

categories.name: Market Dynamics
ideas: Possibility of new tankers being built (entry)
Consolidation or cartel behavior among owners

categories.name: Asset Specifics
ideas: Age and remaining useful life of the tanker
Scrap metal value as a floor
Possibility of converting to alternative cargo
Current charter contract or spot market position

recommendation: Under current demand (500 units/year), the inherited medium tanker has zero financial value beyond scrap value — it is a marginal supplier and earns no economic profit
If demand expands to 650 units/year, the medium tanker becomes inframarginal and would be worth approximately $250,000 (perpetuity of $25,000/year at 10% discount rate)
risks: Demand could remain at or below 500 units, keeping the tanker at zero or scrap value
New large-tanker construction could displace medium tankers even at higher demand levels
Operating costs could rise (fuel, regulation), further eroding profitability
The competitive, fragmented market structure means no pricing power
next_steps: Obtain a professional scrap-value appraisal to establish the floor valuation
Monitor oil demand forecasts to assess probability of Scenario II
Explore whether chartering the tanker short-term can lock in revenue before any demand shift
Consider whether selling to a larger fleet operator commands any synergy premium
